## What is a Bloom filter? {background-image="figures/static/bloom1970.png" background-size="contain" background-position="right" background-opacity="0.5"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Published in 1970 by Burton H. Bloom
- A space-efficient, probabilistic set data structure
- False positives are possible; false negatives are not
- Trades a small error rate for significantly less memory usage
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
- How many people know or have used Bloom filter(s)?
- Paper: memory too small → accept some false "yes" to shrink the hash table
  - Example: hyphenation, 10% of words need disk
  - 2M bits → <300k bits, 84% fewer disk reads
:::

## Example: inserting elements {.hide-title .center}

{{< include figures/out/blackbox_stack.md >}}

::: {.notes}
- Hash function choice doesn't matter too much. Faster is better. Secure is unnecessary
- Because we hash elements, their size inside the Bloom filter is unrelated to their original size
- We can't retrieve elements from the filter. We can only test their presence when we have the element
:::

## Where are Bloom filters used?

```{=html}
<div class="uses">
  <img src="figures/out/uses/db.svg">
  <div><strong>Database query optimization</strong><span>Skip disk reads and join lookups that can't match</span></div>
  <img src="figures/out/uses/git.svg">
  <div><strong>Git log</strong><span>Skip commits that didn't touch a file: <code>git log -- README.md</code></span></div>
  <img src="figures/out/uses/dna.svg">
  <div><strong>DNA sequence algorithms</strong><span>Store huge sets of k-mers (short DNA substrings) in memory</span></div>
  <img src="figures/out/uses/url.svg">
  <div><strong>Malicious URL detection</strong><span>Check URLs locally; ask the server only on a "maybe"</span></div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
- They're often used to avoid a costly action
- Generally when you're dealing with lots of data and/or statistical algorithms
- They can also be used in memory-restricted/embedded systems, e.g. network hardware or CPU caches
:::

## Git: faster file history {.git-slide}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Each commit stores a Bloom filter of the **paths it changed**
- `git log -- <file>` checks each commit's filter first
  - "definitely not" → skip the tree diff
  - "maybe" → diff to confirm
- Off by default: enable once per repo
- Test repo: 1000 commits, 7 false positives → 0.7% false-positive rate
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
```{=html}
<pre class="terminal small-term"><span class="prompt">$</span> git commit-graph write --reachable --changed-paths

<span class="prompt">$</span> git log --oneline -- README.md
5509d4a Update README
1a2a47d Add README

<span class="prompt">$</span> GIT_TRACE2_PERF=1 git log --oneline -- README.md 2&gt;&amp;1 \
    | grep -o 'statistics.*'
statistics:{"filter_not_present":0,"maybe":9,
            <span class="hl">"definitely_not":990</span>,<span class="hl">"false_positive":7</span>}</pre>
<p class="caption-small">990 of 1000 commits skipped without a diff</p>
```
:::
::::

## False positives during assembly

![](figures/out/fp_branches.svg){width="100%"}

- A false positive lets the assembler step off the real sequence
- The next k-mers on that branch aren't in the reads either → it dies after a few bases
- Short dead-end branches are simply ignored

## How many hash functions?

{{< include figures/out/optimal_k_stack.md >}}

::: {.notes}
- FP rate calculation is inexact because we dunno how many bits overlap

Derivation (n elements, m bits, k hashes):

1. One hash sets a given bit with prob 1/m → bit stays 0: (1 − 1/m)
2. After n inserts = kn bit-sets: P(bit still 0) = (1 − 1/m)^(kn) ≈ e^(−kn/m)
3. Non-member is a FP if all k of its bits are 1: FP ≈ (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k
4. Optimum: write p = e^(−kn/m) (fraction of 0 bits). Then ln FP = −(m/n)·ln p·ln(1 − p), symmetric in p and 1 − p → minimum at p = 1/2
5. e^(−kn/m) = 1/2 → k = (m/n)·ln 2. At the optimum, half the bits are 1, and FP = (1/2)^k
:::
